absent: Exact numeric values of thread limits, marker constants, filter masks and shifts.
Complete field layout, sizes and offsets of task, address space and signal descriptors beyond observed uses.
Locking discipline for address space list and mapping locks beyond initialization and observed read write usage.
Behaviour of cross dossier helpers for allocation, barriers, reference counts and security checks.
Scheduling, cgroup, security and accounting teardown details beyond that they are invoked during task release.
Full virtual fork completion protocol and who signals completion.
Architecture specific overrides for task duplication, caches and thread state whitelists.
Error code values and user visible effects beyond success versus failure distinctions observed.

findings.text: Address space lifetime and inspection operations are provided for other subsystems, covering creation, final release, asynchronous release, executable tracking replacement and controlled access to another task descriptor.
Task release, deferred release, inspection permission, shadow stack allocation and per task messaging mask allocation are provided for use by core kernel subsystems.

Final release entry for an address space descriptor after its last reference drops. It refuses the initial descriptor, ensures no processor still uses it as a lazy descriptor, tears down scheduling, paging, identity, notification and accounting state, validates counters, then returns storage to its cache.

An address space being freed is expected to have zero resident counters of every type and zero page table accounting. Observed violations are reported as alerts naming the descriptor, counter type, value and current task identity, but do not stop teardown. A huge page table pointer is also expected to be clear where applicable.

Lazy processor usage of an address space is revoked before free when the relevant configuration is enabled. Each processor whose mask still references the descriptor is asked to switch its active descriptor to the initial one if it matches, with warnings if inconsistencies are seen. A debug option rechecks all processors afterwards. When the configuration is off the step is a no operation.

Address space descriptors are obtained from and returned to a dedicated slab cache for this type. Allocation may fail and is checked by callers; freeing assumes a valid descriptor from the same cache.

Final drops of address space references can be deferred to process context through a work item embedded in the descriptor. If decrementing the relevant count reaches zero, a work item is initialized and scheduled; the work handler then performs the final release. One variant guards the overall pin count and the other guards the user mapping count, separating atomic decrement from potentially blocking teardown.

Shared signal state has reference counted lifetime. Last release frees thread group statistics and scheduling group state, defers release of any retained out of memory target descriptor to asynchronous context, then returns the structure to its cache.

Final task descriptor release requires the task to have exited and to have no remaining usage references, and it must not be the current task; violations are warned about. Teardown releases scheduling, security and credential state together with grouping, memory policy, messaging, accounting, unwinding and shared signal state before freeing the descriptor itself. A read copy update callback wrapper allows this release from deferred reclamation context.

Architecture hook for early task cache initialization with a default empty implementation that may be overridden by architecture code. It is invoked during early fork subsystem setup and has no effect unless overridden.

Maximum thread count is derived from estimated free memory divided by per thread stack cost with a safety divisor, bounded above by a suggested ceiling and clamped within global minimum and maximum limits. The computation avoids overflow by checking bit lengths before multiplying.
The size used for task descriptor allocation is held in a global that is expected to be set by architecture code before slab creation and thereafter treated as mostly read.

Early initialization covers slab creation for task descriptors with cache aware alignment and a user copy whitelist derived from architecture thread state, architecture cache setup, thread limit computation, seeding of initial resource limits and user namespace counters from those limits, configuration of selected namespace ceilings as unlimited, and registration of stack cache cleanup, shadow stack, lock tracking and probe subsystems.
Shadow stack subsystem initialization is a no operation when the feature is disabled; otherwise it registers a per processor cleanup callback for the shadow stack cache during early boot.
Architecture hook for duplicating a task descriptor with a default that copies the whole descriptor and reports success, allowing architectures to override with additional handling.
Each task stack carries a trailing marker value used to detect overflow. The marker is written at the computed stack end during task duplication; corruption observed later indicates stack overflow.

Task duplication allocates a new descriptor and stack on a selected memory node, copies architecture state, establishes stack accounting, messaging mask and shadow stack resources, clears scheduling, notification and dispatch state, establishes fresh reference counts and nulls deferred pointers, inherits CPU affinity and initializes tracing, fault and accounting state. Any allocation or preparation failure unwinds already acquired resources and returns no descriptor.
Coverage state for a new task starts from a reset baseline, clears remote and soft interrupt tracking plus saved mode and area state, and inherits the current coverage handle.
Memory node selection for task duplication defaults to no preference except that the kernel thread daemon may direct its children to its preferred fork node under non uniform memory configurations.

Shadow stack attachment is skipped when disabled. Otherwise a stack is obtained first from a small per processor cache of cleared reusable stacks, falling back to virtual allocation on the requested node when the cache is empty. New stacks receive an end marker, poisoning for debugging allocators and accounting before being attached as both base and current pointer; allocation failure is reported to the caller.
Per task inter processor interrupt mask storage is unnecessary when masks are inlined. Otherwise a mask sized allocation is attempted and failure is reported.
A globally shared spinlock aligned to avoid cache line contention protects the list linking all address space descriptors.

Default core dump filtering mask is configurable via an early boot parameter that is parsed as an integer, shifted into position and masked to allowed bits; unparsable input leaves the prior default unchanged.

New address space construction zeroes the descriptor, initializes mapping tree, reference counts, sequencing, locking, lists and accounting, prepares input output, ownership, probe, huge page and futex state, inherits filtering and default mapping flags from the current descriptor when present, then acquires paging, identity, context and scheduling resources plus per processor counters. Ownership can later be cleared when it matches a departing task. Any acquisition failure releases already acquired resources and returns no descriptor.

Executable file replacement first inspects mappings under a read lock and refuses with a busy status if the old file remains mapped. Write access to the new file is then denied and a reference is taken before swapping the tracked pointer under a write lock; the old file if any is then allowed writes again and released.

Access to another task address space requires holding that thread group execution update lock in read mode while obtaining and validating the descriptor. Access is always allowed for the current descriptor, otherwise it requires ptrace permission or, for read mode, a performance monitoring capability; denial releases the reference and reports access failure, while missing descriptors report absence and interrupted locks report interruption.

Permission to inspect a task is decided under the task lock with read copy update protection for credentials. Same thread group access is always allowed. Otherwise exactly one credential mode must be selected; the caller filesystem or real identifiers are compared against all target user and group identities, falling back to a system ptrace capability in the target user namespace. A memory ordering barrier then separates credential sampling from dumpability sampling, where owner dumpable tasks pass and others again require the capability in the execution namespace before consulting the security module.

Task structure locking serializes credential checks for inspection and clearing of parent child rendezvous state when a virtual fork wait is interrupted. Locks are held only for the minimal check or update and released before returning.

A parent waiting for virtual fork completion enters a frozen aware killable and freezable sleep on a completion object, leaving frozen state on wake. If the wait is interrupted, the child rendezvous pointer is cleared under lock. The child reference is released in all cases and interruption status is returned.

Observed task descriptor state includes stack and shadow stack tracking, CPU affinity pointers, reference and read copy update counts, scheduling, execution, coverage, tracing and accounting fields plus pointers for messaging, pipes, fragments, work queues and filtering. Duplication establishes fresh counts and clears deferred pointers while teardown releases the associated subsystems.

Observed address space descriptor state includes a mapping tree with external lock, user and pin reference counts, sequencing for write protection, mapping list linkage, page table and resident accounting, page table and argument locks, processor mask, input output table, ownership, execution file pointer, notification subscriptions, flush pending state and work item for deferred release. Teardown validates that accounting has drained.

Several misuse conditions trigger diagnostics rather than silent corruption: releasing the initial address space or the current descriptors, releasing a task with remaining references or without exit state, finding unexpected active descriptor relationships during lazy revocation, and requesting inspection without selecting a credential mode. Each is reported via warnings or alerts.
The implementation defines STACK_END_MAGIC as a stack boundary marker written during task creation for overflow detection.
The implementation defines SCS_END_MAGIC as a shadow stack marker written at allocation to detect corruption.

The implementation defines MIN_THREADS and MAX_THREADS as bounds for thread count computation, with RLIMIT_NPROC and RLIMIT_SIGPENDING plus UCOUNT_RLIMIT_MEMLOCK, UCOUNT_RLIMIT_MSGQUEUE, UCOUNT_RLIMIT_NPROC and UCOUNT_RLIMIT_SIGPENDING as resource and namespace identifiers seeded from the computed limit.

The implementation defines MMF_DUMP_FILTER_DEFAULT with MMF_DUMP_FILTER_SHIFT and MMF_DUMP_FILTER_MASK for boot configuration of dump filtering, plus VM_INIT_DEF_MASK for inheriting mapping defaults in new address spaces.

The implementation defines PTRACE_MODE_READ, PTRACE_MODE_FSCREDS, PTRACE_MODE_REALCREDS and PTRACE_MODE_NOAUDIT as inspection mode bits, with CAP_SYS_PTRACE as the overriding capability and TASK_DUMPABLE_OWNER as a dumpability state that bypasses further checks.
The implementation defines TASK_KILLABLE and TASK_FREEZABLE as sleep states used when a parent blocks for virtual fork completion.

New address space locking initializes a read write semaphore for mappings with an associated sequence counter and, where supported, a wait queue for writers, plus spinlocks for page tables, arguments and asynchronous input output.
Initial mapping and filtering defaults for a new address space are inherited from the current descriptor when one exists, otherwise they start from global defaults and zero.
